archetype.name: Playoff Team (possession-driven)
archetype.definition: A club coming off a deep playoff run that is now controlling 5-on-5 play better than it ever has, but is waiting for its goaltending and shooting to catch up.

report.headline: Montréal is finally winning the puck; the saves and power play haven't followed yet
report.take:
Six games in, Montréal looks like a more complete hockey team that is getting worse results. The record is 3-2-1 and the site has the Canadiens 21st, with a Goal Diff / GP of -0.5 that sits 21st as well. Underneath that is the best territorial profile this group has shown in years. A 55.0 CF % ranks 5th and a 54.9 xGF % ranks 8th. For context, last season's 48-24-10 team that won nine playoff games did it with a 47.9 xGF % and a 49.0 CF %. It was outchanced and won anyway on 22.4 goals saved above expected and a 101.8 PDO.

This year that formula has flipped. The Canadiens are driving play, but the goaltending sits at -2.1 GSAx (23rd) and the PDO is 96. A team out-chancing opponents by this margin while shooting and saving this poorly is usually a team whose goal differential is about to improve. The split in net drives most of it. Jacob Fowler has a .906 save %, 1.8 GSAx and a shutout over three starts. Jakub Dobes is at .856 and -4 GSAx over his three. The three-game losing streak came in games where Montréal scored 4 and 5 and still lost, which points at the back end rather than the attack.

The skaters look like last year's core. Nick Suzuki has 8 points while playing 22.32 minutes, and Lane Hutson logs 26.82 minutes with 6 points and ranks 16th among 239 defensemen. Zachary Bolduc has three goals in under 14 minutes a night. Two things cut against the optimism. The power play is converting 10% (30th), a sharp drop from last year's 23.1%. And a Pts vs Goal Diff of +1.3 (6th) says the record is already a little ahead of the goals. The recent pattern of a one-goal win, a shutout and a one-goal win is not something to lean on.

The direction is still encouraging. Montréal has gone from 31st on the site in 2021-22 to 6th last season, and the underlying play now matches that climb more honestly than it did a year ago. If Fowler keeps the crease and the power play reaches even a league-normal rate, the goal differential should turn positive. In that case 21st on the site will look like a six-game artifact.

strengths.title: Owning the puck at 5-on-5
strengths.body: A 55.0 CF % (5th) and 54.9 xGF % (8th) mean Montréal is spending more time in the offensive zone and creating the better chances. That is a real change from last season's 47.9 xGF %, when the team was outchanced and survived on goaltending. Six games is a small sample, but shot-share numbers stabilize faster than goals do, so this is the most trustworthy number on the sheet.

strengths.title: Suzuki and Hutson carry the minutes
strengths.body: Suzuki leads the team with 8 points and plays 22.32 minutes. Hutson plays 26.82 minutes a night with 6 points and a 59.5 xGF % on his ice time. Both rank near the top of their position tabs. These are the two players the possession edge runs through, and their production looks driven by usage rather than luck.

strengths.title: Depth wingers finishing chances
strengths.body: Bolduc has 3 goals on 11 shots and a 65.4 xGF % in 13.89 minutes. Josh Anderson's line is at 69.9 xGF %. The bottom of the lineup is not just surviving; it is winning its minutes. Bolduc's finishing rate will cool, but the chance share behind it should hold up.

concerns.title: A goaltending split that costs games
concerns.body: Fowler (.906, 1.8 GSAx) and Dobes (.856, -4 GSAx) have split the six starts evenly, and the team total of -2.1 GSAx ranks 23rd. That drags a C- goaltending grade onto a team that was winning on saves a year ago. The fix is either Dobes rebounding or Fowler taking the bulk of the starts; neither is guaranteed on six games of evidence.

concerns.title: Power play stuck at 10%
concerns.body: At 10% the power play ranks 30th, and the forwards have only 4 PP points between them. This is the same core that converted 23.1% last season, so the talent says this rises. Until it does, the 5-on-5 edge is being given back on special teams.

concerns.title: Opposing defensemen getting loose
concerns.body: Opposing defensemen are scoring 3.5 points a game against Montréal against an expected 2 (rank 30). They account for 32.8% of the points against, versus a league share of 24.8%. That points to point shots and activated blueliners getting through, which fits a team losing the goaltending battle on shots it should be stopping. Some of it is save-percentage noise, but it is worth watching.

trend.note: A win in Toronto, then three straight losses while allowing five or six goals, then three wins in a row including a 1-0 shutout of Detroit. The swings have tracked the goaltending more than the play.

weekAhead.headline: One test in Washington, then two home games against weak teams
weekAhead.body:
The week opens in Washington against a 3-3-0 Capitals team that is the best opponent on the slate mainly because of its goaltending. Washington has +6.1 GSAx (3rd) and a 103.4 PDO, while its own play is middling: 50.6 xGF %, 48.0 CF %, and a D+ forwards grade. Montréal should out-possess the Capitals. The question is whether it can solve a hot goalie, and that is the toughest of the three games.

Then come two home games. Buffalo, beaten 4-3 on Tuesday, matches Montréal's 54.9 xGF % but has a D goaltending grade, -3.9 GSAx and a 60.9 PK %. San Jose has a 37.3 xGF % (31st) and D grades in every group. Both are the kind of opponent a possession team should beat at home, and Buffalo's penalty kill is the best chance all week for the power play to get going.

keyMatchups.title: Power play vs Buffalo's penalty kill
keyMatchups.body: Montréal's power play converts 10% (30th), and Buffalo kills only 60.9% of penalties (30th). One of those numbers has to give. If the Canadiens can't score with the extra man against this kill, the slump becomes a real problem rather than early noise.

keyMatchups.title: Shot volume against Washington's goalie
keyMatchups.body: Washington ranks 3rd in GSAx with a 103.4 PDO, the mirror image of Montréal's 96. The Canadiens' 55.0 CF % should tilt the ice. Whether that turns into goals depends on Washington's goaltending cooling off. Washington also holds defensemen well under expectation (rank 3), so Hutson's offense may be harder to come by here.

keyMatchups.title: San Jose's lack of possession
keyMatchups.body: The Sharks have a 37.3 xGF % and a 91.5 PDO, and they allow 1.38 points a game above expectation to forwards. This is a game Montréal's forwards should control. It is also a good chance for the defense to cut down the chances it has been giving opposing defensemen.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in net. Fowler's .906 and Dobes' .856 is the biggest gap on the roster, and the week's results will likely follow it.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying play says this team should finish with a positive goal differential and a playoff spot, and possibly a better true profile than last year's. Last season's success rested on goaltending and PDO that tend not to repeat. This season the 5-on-5 control is already there, and the goaltending and shooting have room to rise from a 96 PDO. Expect the goal differential to improve as PDO drifts back toward 100. The power play should climb toward its previous level given the same personnel.

What won't last is the edge in close games: a +1.3 Pts vs Goal Diff six games in is noise. The team's previous seasons were also well above its goal differential, so some of last year's record was borrowed. The ceiling depends on the crease. A reliable starter, most plausibly Fowler on early form, makes this a top-ten team on the site again. A season-long split with a struggling partner would keep the Canadiens in the wild-card mix.
swingFactors: Fowler's form and share of the starts
Power play returning toward last year's rate
Holding the 55% shot share over a full season

confidence.note: Six games, and a goalie split that could flip quickly.
